network.overall_strategy: This graph enumerates ten distinct candidate reaction-sequence pathways, not ten experimentally established prebiotic syntheses. Six combine two precursor-entry reactions with three alternative ring-building sequences; four explore cyclic-imine and pyrrole routes. The supplied review attributes a cyanosulfidic route to Patel et al. (2015), but its deoxygenation and thione-to-aminonitrile equations omit reducing equivalents, and its structures do not establish L-selectivity. Those problems are corrected or explicitly identified below. References to that paper distinguish review-level attribution from substrate-specific evidence. Unsupported extensions are marked speculative. All achiral syntheses produce L-proline together with D-proline; no demonstrated prebiotic enantiomeric resolution is assumed. Organic feedstocks are explicit boundary inputs: especially propanedial, butanedial and 2,5-dioxopentanoic acid have unresolved prebiotic supply and concentration. Thus, this is a complete specification of a conditional reaction graph, not a demonstrated continuous synthesis from C1 feedstocks. Proposed conditions are not experimentally verified optima. Incompatible photochemical, hydrogenation and hydrolysis stages require separation, transport or environmental cycling. Null formation environments indicate imported species or formation in multiple settings. The schema's intermediate role also accommodates unavoidable byproducts.

reactions.name: Ammonia conjugate addition to acrolein

conditions.other: Anoxic pool; approximately pH 8-10; rapid downstream trapping would be required to limit secondary reactions.

reactions.mechanism: Aza-Michael addition of ammonia at the beta carbon of acrolein, followed by proton transfer, gives 3-aminopropanal.
reactions.reasoning: The supplied review proposes this precursor entry in the context of Patel et al. (2015), but provides no independently verifiable substrate-specific experiment. Treat its geochemical operation as speculative. Conjugate addition is chemically reasonable, while competing carbonyl condensation, multiple additions and oligomerization make selective accumulation uncertain.

reactions.name: Monoreductive amination of propanedial
agents: Accessible native nickel-iron alloy surfaces, such as awaruite; proposed catalyst

conditions.pressure: Elevated hydrothermal pressure with dissolved H2
conditions.other: Anoxic, approximately pH 7-9; sulfur-poor microenvironment needed to reduce catalyst passivation.

reactions.mechanism: One aldehyde condenses with ammonia, and hydrogenation of the resulting imine produces the amino aldehyde with net water release.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative. The supplied review mentions this precursor possibility without establishing a working prebiotic reaction. Nickel-bearing metal surfaces are chemically relevant to H2 activation, but their activity and selectivity here are unverified. Dialdehyde hydration, direct carbonyl reduction, diamination and polymerization compete; precursor availability is also unresolved.

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin formation from 3-aminopropanal

conditions.other: Anoxic concentrated solution; approximately pH 7-9, allowing a reactive cyanide fraction while limiting amino-aldehyde decomposition.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to the aldehyde carbonyl and protonation gives the alpha-hydroxynitrile. Addition to either carbonyl face produces racemic material.
reactions.reasoning: Attributed to Patel et al. (2015) by the supplied review; the elementary cyanohydrin chemistry is credible, although the exact experimental attribution has not been independently checked here. This is carbonyl cyanohydrin formation, not the complete ammonia-dependent Strecker reaction. Reversibility and amino-aldehyde instability limit net flux.

reactions.name: Sulfide addition and hydroxylated thiolactam formation

conditions.other: Anoxic sulfide-bearing pool; approximately pH 7-9; low accessible metal loading to limit sulfide precipitation.

reactions.mechanism: Sulfide addition to the nitrile generates thioimidate/thioamide functionality. Intramolecular attack by the terminal amine and ammonia elimination produce a five-membered cyclic thioamide.
reactions.reasoning: The supplied review attributes this transformation to Patel et al. (2015). Five-membered ring closure is structurally plausible, but the attribution does not establish the proposed environmental rate or selectivity. Intermolecular reactions and slow ammonia displacement remain possible bottlenecks; no mineral catalyst is added without evidence.

reactions.name: Proposed photoreductive deoxygenation of the hydroxylated thiolactam
agents: Dissolved copper(I)-cyanide photoredox complexes; substrate-specific activity hypothetical

conditions.other: UV-irradiated anoxic shallow solution; sulfide is the sacrificial electron donor. Sulfur is represented as S8 for idealized net bookkeeping; actual sulfur speciation may include polysulfides.

reactions.mechanism: Hypothesized photoredox electron transfer enables C-O bond cleavage and protonation. Sulfide oxidation supplies the reducing equivalents, with net formation of water and elemental sulfur.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate-specific adaptation of the cyanosulfidic photoredox framework associated with Patel et al. (2015), not an independently verified correction of its experimental procedure. The review's equation omits two reducing equivalents. Including sulfide oxidation restores atom and electron bookkeeping. H2S does not generally justify assuming native copper formation from Cu2+; copper sulfide precipitation is a major competing sink.

reactions.name: Proposed reductive cyanation of pyrrolidine-2-thione
agents: Accessible native nickel-iron alloy surface; hypothetical hydrogenation catalyst

conditions.pressure: Elevated hydrothermal pressure with dissolved H2
conditions.other: Anoxic mixing zone; approximately pH 6-8. Requires cyanide trapping before complete reduction and exceptional resistance to sulfur/cyanide poisoning.

reactions.mechanism: The proposed net reaction combines partial reductive desulfurization with cyanide capture of an imine/iminium equivalent. H2 supplies the otherwise missing hydrogen equivalents; the product is racemic prolinonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative and a major feasibility bottleneck. The supplied review attributes thione-to-nitrile conversion to Patel et al. (2015), but its equation is short by H2 and cannot be simple cyanide displacement as written. This balanced hydrogenative alternative is not established by that citation. Native alloy surfaces are considered only for H2 activation; sulfide poisoning, cyanide binding and overreduction to pyrrolidine may prevent useful conversion.

reactions.name: Proposed cyanohydrin deoxygenation before ring closure
agents: Dissolved copper(I)-cyanide photoredox complexes; proposed catalyst

conditions.other: UV irradiation under anoxic conditions; sulfide supplies reducing equivalents. S8 is an idealized terminal sulfur product.

reactions.mechanism: Hypothesized reductive cleavage of the cyanohydrin C-O bond replaces hydroxyl with hydrogen while retaining the nitrile, giving 4-aminobutanenitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative; the supplied evidence does not demonstrate this substrate-specific transformation. Patel et al. (2015) supports the broader photoredox framework, not selective execution of this branch. It tests a chemically different order of deoxygenation and cyclization. Nitrile reduction, retrocyanohydrin fragmentation and catalyst precipitation may dominate instead.

reactions.name: Direct thiolactam formation from 4-aminobutanenitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic sulfide-bearing pool; approximately pH 7-9; thermal cycling may assist equilibration.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile thiolysis followed by intramolecular aminolysis and ammonia elimination produces pyrrolidine-2-thione directly.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative extension of the nitrile/sulfide ring-forming chemistry attributed to Patel et al. (2015) in the review. The amino-nitrile spacing permits a five-membered ring and avoids deoxygenation of an already sulfur-containing heterocycle. Actual rates and competition with open-chain thioamides are not established by the supplied evidence.

reactions.name: Partial nitrile hydrogenation and intramolecular transimination
agents: Accessible native nickel-iron alloy surface; proposed catalyst

conditions.pressure: Elevated hydrothermal pressure with dissolved H2
conditions.other: Anoxic, sulfur-poor interface; approximately pH 7-9. Product must escape or be trapped before further hydrogenation.

reactions.mechanism: Partial nitrile reduction gives an aldimine equivalent. The terminal amine undergoes intramolecular transimination, releasing ammonia and forming 1-pyrroline.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative; no supporting experiment is provided in the review. The net reaction is balanced and five-membered cyclic imine formation is chemically reasonable. Selective partial hydrogenation is the principal weakness: full reduction to a diamine or subsequent pyrroline reduction can outcompete the desired branch.

reactions.name: Monoreductive amination of butanedial
agents: Accessible native nickel-iron alloy surface; proposed catalyst

conditions.pressure: Elevated hydrothermal pressure with dissolved H2
conditions.other: Anoxic, approximately pH 7-9; low sulfide activity and immediate intramolecular trapping are required.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia condensation at one aldehyde followed by imine hydrogenation produces 4-aminobutanal and water.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative. Reductive amination supplies the correct four-carbon amino-aldehyde skeleton without the cyanosulfidic ring-building sequence. The supplied literature does not establish this prebiotic route or a sustained butanedial source. Dialdehyde polymerization, carbonyl hydrogenation and diamination are important competitors.

reactions.name: Cyclocondensation of 4-aminobutanal

conditions.other: Anoxic interface; approximately pH 6-9; reversible amino-aldehyde/cyclic-imine equilibrium.

reactions.mechanism: Intramolecular amine addition to the aldehyde forms a cyclic hemiaminal, followed by water elimination to 1-pyrroline.
reactions.reasoning: Standard five-membered imine-forming chemistry; its operation within this prebiotic sequence is speculative because it is not documented in the supplied evidence. Cyclization offers a chemically justified sink for an unstable amino aldehyde, but aqueous equilibrium and further hydrogenation limit accumulation.

reactions.name: Strecker-type cyanation of a preformed cyclic imine

conditions.other: Anoxic cyanide-bearing pool; approximately pH 6-8; pyrroline must be captured faster than hydrolysis or oligomerization.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide attacks the cyclic imine/iminium carbon and proton transfer gives pyrrolidine-2-carbonitrile. Attack from either face yields a racemate.
reactions.reasoning: Chemically conventional imine cyanation, but speculative as a complete prebiotic route under the supplied evidence. The review's assertion that Strecker chemistry cannot yield cyclic amino acids is too broad: cyanation of a preformed cyclic imine avoids that limitation. No L-selectivity is implied.

reactions.name: Acid-assisted hydration of prolinonitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic acidic geothermal pool; approximately pH 1-3; prolonged residence may be needed.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile protonation and water addition produce an imidic intermediate that tautomerizes to the primary amide.
reactions.reasoning: The supplied review attributes overall aminonitrile hydrolysis to Patel et al. (2015). Resolving it into hydration and amide hydrolysis exposes a real kinetic bottleneck. The warmer acidic conditions are a proposed geochemical adaptation, not conditions verified by that citation; ambient neutral hydrolysis should not be assumed rapid.

reactions.name: Prolinamide hydrolysis to racemic proline

conditions.other: Anoxic acidic pool; approximately pH 1-3. Ammonia is represented in neutral formula form although ammonium dominates here.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-catalyzed addition-elimination hydrolyzes the primary amide to the carboxylic acid and ammonia. Racemic feed gives equal L- and D-proline outputs; stoichiometric coefficients are implicit.
reactions.reasoning: This resolves the second part of hydrolysis attributed to Patel et al. (2015) in the review. Slow amide cleavage may determine overall residence time. Crucially, neither the provided achiral structures nor hydrolysis establishes L-selectivity. The target is obtained only as the L component of racemic proline, not as an enantiopure product.

reactions.name: Alpha-keto-group reductive amination of 2,5-dioxopentanoic acid
agents: Accessible native nickel-iron alloy surface; proposed catalyst

conditions.pressure: Elevated hydrothermal pressure with dissolved H2
conditions.other: Anoxic, approximately pH 6-9; low sulfide activity. Regioselectivity is not assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia condensation and hydrogenation at the alpha-keto group generate racemic glutamate 5-semialdehyde while retaining the terminal aldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative; no supplied paper demonstrates this selective prebiotic transformation. It provides a chemically recognizable entry to the pyrroline-5-carboxylate skeleton. However, aldehyde amination or reduction may dominate, so this is a possible competing product channel rather than a claimed selective synthesis. The C5 feedstock's prebiotic availability is an independent major gap.

reactions.name: Glutamate-semialdehyde cyclocondensation

conditions.other: Anoxic, approximately pH 6-9; cyclic imine and open-chain aldehyde remain in equilibrium.

reactions.mechanism: The alpha amino group attacks the terminal aldehyde, and dehydration closes the five-membered ring to pyrroline-5-carboxylic acid.
reactions.reasoning: The ring-chain relationship is established chemical logic, but this prebiotic implementation is speculative and is not supported by the supplied Patel et al. (2015) review. Five-membered intramolecular condensation is more credible than invoking an uncatalyzed direct reduction of glutamate's carboxyl group. The existing stereocenter remains racemic.

reactions.name: Hydrogenation of pyrroline-5-carboxylic acid
agents: Accessible native nickel-iron alloy surface; proposed catalyst

conditions.pressure: Elevated hydrothermal pressure with dissolved H2
conditions.other: Anoxic, sulfur-poor microenvironment; approximately pH 6-9.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrogenation of the cyclic imine produces the saturated pyrrolidine ring without requiring reduction of the carboxyl group.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative as a mineral-mediated prebiotic reaction; not demonstrated in the supplied literature. Imine hydrogenation is chemically more accessible than carboxylic-acid or lactam reduction, justifying examination of this branch. Catalyst availability, carboxylate adsorption and competing decomposition remain unquantified. Racemic precursor yields both proline enantiomers.

reactions.name: Terminal-aldehyde reductive amination of 2,5-dioxopentanoic acid
agents: Accessible native nickel-iron alloy surface; proposed catalyst

conditions.pressure: Elevated hydrothermal pressure with dissolved H2
conditions.other: Anoxic, approximately pH 6-9; sulfur-poor interface; the alpha-keto group must survive.

reactions.mechanism: Reductive amination of the terminal aldehyde produces 5-amino-2-oxopentanoic acid, retaining the alpha-keto acid functionality.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative; the supplied literature does not establish this route. Aldehyde reductive amination is chemically plausible and leads to a different ring-closing topology from alpha-keto-group amination. Direct carbonyl hydrogenation, double amination and alpha-keto-acid decomposition compete. Availability of the starting ketoaldehyde acid remains unresolved.

reactions.name: Cyclocondensation to pyrroline-2-carboxylic acid

conditions.other: Anoxic, approximately pH 6-9; reversible intramolecular condensation.

reactions.mechanism: The terminal amine attacks the alpha-keto group; dehydration produces a five-membered cyclic imine whose imine carbon bears the carboxyl substituent.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative prebiotic implementation of standard imine chemistry; no supporting experiment is supplied. This is constitutionally distinct from the pyrroline-5-carboxylate branch and uses the correct amine-carbonyl spacing for five-membered closure. Hydration, imine hydrolysis and keto-acid decomposition constrain accumulation.

reactions.name: Hydrogenation of pyrroline-2-carboxylic acid
agents: Accessible native nickel-iron alloy surface; proposed catalyst

conditions.pressure: Elevated hydrothermal pressure with dissolved H2
conditions.other: Anoxic, sulfur-poor microenvironment; approximately pH 6-9; no chiral catalyst is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrogenation of the planar imine carbon establishes the proline alpha stereocenter. Equivalent attack on either face gives L- and D-proline.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative under prebiotic mineral conditions; the supplied literature provides no demonstration. The required transformation is ordinary imine reduction rather than a difficult carboxyl reduction, but activity of native alloys toward this substrate is unverified. Achiral conditions cannot justify selective L-proline production.

reactions.name: Paal-Knorr condensation to pyrrole-2-carboxylic acid
agents: Hydronium ions for general acid catalysis

conditions.other: Anoxic concentrating pool with wet-dry cycling; mildly acidic wet phase. Two water equivalents are produced, without repeated output IDs.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia condenses with the 1,4-dicarbonyl unit, followed by cyclization and two dehydrations to the aromatic pyrrole ring.
reactions.reasoning: The reaction class is chemically established, but this specific prebiotic substrate-and-environment combination is speculative and unsupported by the supplied review. The ketoaldehyde has the required 1,4-dicarbonyl topology. Aromatization could provide a persistent intermediate during concentration; keto-acid decarboxylation, polymerization and uncertain feedstock supply are major limitations.

reactions.name: Hydrogenation of pyrrole-2-carboxylic acid to proline
agents: Accessible native nickel-iron alloy surface; hypothetical aromatic-ring hydrogenation catalyst

conditions.pressure: Elevated hydrothermal pressure with substantial dissolved H2
conditions.other: Anoxic, sulfur-poor interface; stronger hydrogenating conditions than for imine reduction are likely required.

reactions.mechanism: Addition of two H2 equivalents per pyrrole ring saturates both carbon-carbon unsaturations, yielding racemic pyrrolidine-2-carboxylic acid.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative as a geochemical reaction; the supplied literature does not establish it. Pyrrole-ring hydrogenation is chemically possible, but natural alloy performance cannot be inferred from laboratory hydrogenation catalysts. Aromatic stabilization, nitrogen binding, sulfur poisoning and decarboxylation may make this branch ineffective. It is a lower-confidence alternative, not evidence of an additional demonstrated prebiotic route.

pathways.name: Acrolein entry through the hydroxylated-thiolactam sequence
pathways.description: Acrolein supplies 3-aminopropanal, followed by cyanohydrin formation, sulfur-assisted ring closure, proposed deoxygenation and reductive cyanation, then hydrolysis. Closest to the supplied review's framework, but corrected redox steps remain unverified. Produces L-proline with D-proline.

pathways.name: Propanedial entry through the hydroxylated-thiolactam sequence
pathways.description: Speculative monoreductive amination replaces acrolein conjugate addition as the precursor entry. The subsequent thiolactam route shares P1's redox and selectivity bottlenecks and ends in racemic proline.

pathways.name: Acrolein entry with deoxygenation before thiolactam closure
pathways.description: A speculative order-of-operations alternative: remove the cyanohydrin hydroxyl before sulfide-assisted ring formation. This is chemically distinct from deoxygenating the cyclic thioamide, but selective cyanohydrin deoxygenation is unestablished.

pathways.name: Propanedial entry with deoxygenation before thiolactam closure
pathways.description: Combines speculative propanedial monoreductive amination with early cyanohydrin deoxygenation and direct thiolactam formation. It is a distinct complete reaction sequence, not an independently demonstrated synthesis.

pathways.name: Acrolein entry through nitrile reduction and cyclic-imine cyanation
pathways.description: After proposed cyanohydrin deoxygenation, partial nitrile hydrogenation and transimination form pyrroline without a thiolactam intermediate. Cyclic-imine cyanation and hydrolysis yield both proline enantiomers. Avoiding overreduction is a major unresolved requirement.

pathways.name: Propanedial entry through nitrile reduction and cyclic-imine cyanation
pathways.description: Speculative propanedial reductive amination feeds the partial-nitrile-reduction branch. This route bypasses sulfur incorporation into the ring, although sulfide is still consumed in the proposed upstream photodeoxygenation.

pathways.name: Butanedial reductive amination and cyclic Strecker route
pathways.description: A sulfur-independent ring-building candidate: butanedial gives 4-aminobutanal, which cyclizes to pyrroline before cyanide addition and hydrolysis. Feedstock availability and selective monoamination are unresolved; the final product is racemic.

pathways.name: Ketoaldehyde acid through glutamate semialdehyde
pathways.description: Conditional on a supply of 2,5-dioxopentanoic acid, alpha-keto reductive amination gives racemic glutamate semialdehyde. Cyclocondensation and imine hydrogenation produce L- and D-proline without cyanide. Regioselectivity and mineral-catalyzed reduction are speculative.

pathways.name: Ketoaldehyde acid through 5-amino-2-oxopentanoic acid
pathways.description: The alternative reductive-amination regiochemistry generates a terminal amine, followed by pyrroline-2-carboxylate formation and reduction. This is distinct from the glutamate-semialdehyde route, but remains a conditional, unverified prebiotic pathway.

pathways.name: Paal-Knorr aromatization followed by pyrrole hydrogenation
pathways.description: The same conditional ketoaldehyde-acid feedstock undergoes ammonia-driven aromatic ring formation, then hydrogenation in a separate H2-rich setting. This lower-confidence pathway tests an aromatic storage intermediate; no effective natural catalyst or overall prebiotic synthesis is established.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The route is connected and conserves atoms with the supplied coefficients. Its principal bottlenecks are rxn_005 and rxn_006: supplying reducing equivalents fixes their equations but does not establish selective deoxygenation or reductive cyanation. Competing thione reduction/desulfurization and cyanide/sulfide inhibition of candidate hydrogenation catalysts remain unresolved. The final hydrolyses could produce an L-containing racemate if prolinonitrile were obtained, but their required acidity, temperature and residence time are unspecified.
suggestions: Establish rxn_005 and rxn_006 experimentally on the named substrates, including competing products and sulfur fate.
Specify photochemical conditions, a geochemically realistic hydrogenation catalyst, and transfer procedures addressing catalyst passivation and intermediate loss.
Measure acrolein monoaddition selectivity, thiolactam formation and both hydrolysis rates under the proposed conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Accepting propanedial as an explicit boundary input, rxn_002 is formally reasonable but lacks evidence for selective monoamination rather than carbonyl reduction, further amination or condensation. Reactive aminoaldehyde delivery to the surface stage is also unspecified. The downstream deoxygenation and reductive cyanation remain the dominant unresolved transformations. All equations are balanceable; these concerns concern selectivity, kinetics and environmental implementation rather than conservation.
suggestions: Quantify propanedial stability and selective monoamination using a specified catalyst, H2 fugacity and aqueous composition.
Demonstrate the proposed deoxygenation and reductive cyanation rather than relying on their corrected stoichiometry.
Document aminoaldehyde transfer and hydrolysis conditions with measured intermediate survival and product yields.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Cyanohydrin formation and five-membered thiolactam construction provide a coherent formal route. However, rxn_007 requires selective C–O cleavage while retaining the nitrile, and neither H2S consumption nor sulfur formation establishes that selectivity. Thiolactam formation needs substrate-specific kinetic support, and rxn_006 remains a particularly weak link. Hydrolysis would yield racemic proline, including L-proline, but productive flux through the preceding steps is not demonstrated.
suggestions: Test rxn_007 against cyanohydrin dissociation, nitrile reduction and other photochemical products.
Measure thiolactam formation and identify a selective, environmentally credible implementation of rxn_006.
Specify compartment chemistry, catalyst compatibility and sufficient residence time for complete hydrolysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway has consistent molecule identities and balanceable equations, but combines uncertain propanedial monoamination with two unsupported selective reductions. Neither aminoaldehyde availability after rxn_002 nor productive deoxygenation in rxn_007 is established. The proposed thione-to-aminonitrile conversion remains unresolved even after inclusion of H2. Acknowledging these limitations is appropriate, but does not demonstrate a functioning synthesis.
suggestions: Establish selective monoamination and aminoaldehyde survival at stated concentrations and hydrothermal conditions.
Obtain substrate-specific evidence for rxn_007, rxn_008 and especially rxn_006.
Provide a physical transfer scenario and measured hydrolysis conditions rather than environment labels alone.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Cyanation of a preformed cyclic imine is chemically well founded and provides a credible connection to prolinonitrile. Access to that imine is the main problem: rxn_007 is speculative, while rxn_009 must stop nitrile hydrogenation at a stage permitting cyclization without subsequently reducing pyrroline to pyrrolidine. Catalyst choice and timely removal from hydrogenating conditions are therefore consequential. The final steps can produce L-proline as part of a racemate.
suggestions: Demonstrate selective cyanohydrin deoxygenation while retaining the nitrile.
Identify conditions for rxn_009 that favor cyclic-imine formation over complete hydrogenation, and quantify the product distribution.
Show that pyrroline survives transfer to cyanation conditions and establish subsequent nitrile and amide hydrolysis rates.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The cyclic-imine cyanation and hydrolysis segment is chemically credible. Upstream, selective propanedial monoamination, cyanohydrin deoxygenation and partial nitrile hydrogenation are not demonstrated under specified conditions. In particular, H2 availability alone does not establish selective production and preservation of pyrroline. The graph reaches racemic proline formally, but actual production depends on resolving these upstream selectivity and transfer problems.
suggestions: Measure monoamination selectivity and reactive intermediate lifetimes starting from the stated propanedial input.
Validate rxn_007 and selective imine production in rxn_009 with explicit catalysts and product balances.
Specify conditions that preserve pyrroline during transfer and complete both hydrolysis stages.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a credible conditional route: 4-aminobutanal cyclization, cyclic-imine cyanation and aminonitrile hydrolysis are sound transformations. The main bottleneck is selective formation of the aminoaldehyde and preservation of pyrroline during rxn_010–rxn_011, since continued hydrogenation can produce pyrrolidine instead. Competing dialdehyde chemistry and pyrroline loss during transfer also require evaluation. No demonstrated catalyst conditions or integrated yields are supplied. Racemic production nevertheless includes the requested L enantiomer.
suggestions: Demonstrate productive butanedial monoamination and cyclization while quantifying pyrrolidine, direct carbonyl-reduction products and condensation products.
Specify how pyrroline leaves hydrogenating conditions and is trapped by cyanide before hydrolysis or oligomerization.
Provide substrate-specific evidence and realistic pH, temperature and residence times for complete conversion to proline.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Glutamate-semialdehyde cyclization and subsequent imine reduction constitute a chemically coherent route. The weak point is selective alpha-keto reductive amination of a substrate also containing an aldehyde; catalyst identity, competing carbonyl reduction and substrate stability are unspecified. Terminal-aldehyde amination is not necessarily a network-level loss because P9 consumes that product. Hydrogenation of racemic pyrroline-5-carboxylic acid would preserve access to both proline enantiomers, but the proposed environmental implementation remains unverified.
suggestions: Determine the product distribution of ketoaldehyde reductive amination, including both network-recognized regioisomers and genuinely unproductive products.
Specify a realistic catalyst, its mineral or metallic state, H2 fugacity, pH and temperature for the reductive steps.
Measure in situ cyclization and proline formation, including ketoaldehyde stability and possible decarboxylation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Accepting the stated ketoaldehyde boundary input, this is the strongest conditional pathway. Terminal-aldehyde reductive amination, five-membered imine formation and imine hydrogenation are mechanistically credible, and continued imine reduction here gives the desired product rather than diverting it. Nevertheless, selective amination and productive H2 activation by an environmentally available catalyst have not been demonstrated. Competing carbonyl reduction, further amination and substrate decomposition remain unresolved. The expected racemate contains L-proline but establishes no enantiomeric enrichment.
suggestions: Demonstrate rxn_018–rxn_020 with the named substrate and quantify flux into proline versus competing products.
Document catalyst availability and activity under specified temperature, pH, H2 fugacity and water composition.
Provide primary experimental references or explicitly retain this branch as an unverified proposal, and measure product identity, yield and enantiomeric composition.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The ketoaldehyde has the required 1,4-dicarbonyl arrangement for a Paal–Knorr condensation, and rxn_021 correctly releases two waters. Pyrrole saturation is also balanced at two H2 per substrate, but aromatic-ring hydrogenation requires a suitable active catalyst and is more demanding than the imine reductions in P8 and P9. No supporting catalyst, pressure or substrate-specific performance is supplied. Decarboxylation and other decomposition during processing must be assessed. Successful hydrogenation would produce racemic proline.
suggestions: Verify pyrrole-2-carboxylic acid formation and retention of its carboxyl group under the proposed condensation conditions.
Demonstrate rxn_022 with an environmentally realistic catalyst and explicit H2 fugacity, temperature and reaction time.
Measure intermediate survival during transfer and distinguish proline formation from decarboxylation or ring-degradation products.

evaluation.network_feedback: The graph has high structural validity: it contains sufficient nodes, is connected, uses molecule IDs consistently, and has no conservation violations under the supplied deterministic check. All 22 reactions are balanced or balanceable. Coefficients associated with S8 and separate L/D product nodes are ordinary stoichiometric bookkeeping, not pathological requirements. The explicit organic boundary inputs and racemic products are appropriately disclosed; neither failure to start from C1 compounds nor absence of enantiopurity is independently disqualifying. Racemic production counts as production of an L-proline component. Chemically, P7–P9 provide credible conditional routes, with P9 strongest, but no branch has sufficiently specified and supported conditions for high-confidence target production. Principal unresolved transformations are rxn_005, rxn_006 and rxn_007, together with selective partial hydrogenation in rxn_009 and aromatic hydrogenation in rxn_022. Competition between rxn_015 and rxn_018 need not be fatal because both products have downstream routes to proline. Environmental labels and acknowledgement of transfer requirements do not establish catalyst activity, compatible solution chemistry, intermediate survival or sufficient residence times. Literature alignment is partial: the network correctly identifies the review's redox and stereochemical problems, but review-level attribution to Patel et al. (2015) does not verify the revised transformations or additional branches. Reaction-specific primary evidence, conditions and yields are needed. Overall, this is a transparent, balanced hypothesis network rather than an established synthesis and is not approved at the 0.9 network-confidence threshold.
